title: Keilah Saved, Ziph Betrays, Jonathan Strengthens
summary: David inquires of the LORD and rescues the town of Keilah from Philistine raiders, but when Saul prepares to besiege him there, the LORD reveals through the ephod that Keilah's people would hand David over, and David escapes. In the Wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan comes to strengthen David in God and they renew their covenant. The Ziphites betray David to Saul, who closes in around a mountain in the Wilderness of Maon, until news of a Philistine raid calls Saul away at the last moment.
story: Chapter 22 ended with Abiathar, sole survivor of Nob, joining David. Chapter 23 shows why that mattered: David now has the ephod, the means of seeking God's guidance, and he uses it repeatedly, while Saul, who destroyed the priests, has cut himself off from it. David acts like a king already, defending an Israelite town from the Philistines, which was supposed to be Saul's task (9:16). Yet the people he protects would betray him, and his own tribe of Judah informs on him. The chapter also contains the last meeting between David and Jonathan. After this Jonathan appears only in the report of his death (chapter 31).
historical:
Keilah was a walled town in the lowlands of Judah, a few miles south of Adullam, close to the Philistine border. The Philistines raided such towns at harvest, when grain was gathered on the threshing floors and easy to carry off. Ziph and Maon lay in the dry hill country south of Hebron, bordering the Judean wilderness, a region of rough terrain, caves, and few settlements, well suited to hiding. Jeshimon, meaning wasteland, probably refers to the desolate slopes that run down toward the Dead Sea.

The heading of Psalm 54 connects that psalm with the Ziphites' report to Saul, and it is a prayer for deliverance from strangers and ruthless men who seek the psalmist's life. The place name Sela-hammahlekoth (verse 28) is usually explained as the rock of parting or the rock of escape, recalling how Saul and David were separated just as Saul was closing in. En-gedi (verse 29) was an oasis with springs on the western shore of the Dead Sea, surrounded by cliffs and caves.
cultural:
Threshing floors were flat, open areas, often on high ground to catch the wind, where harvested grain was beaten and then tossed so the wind carried away the chaff. At harvest, a year's food lay exposed there, which made them a prime target for raiders. Walled towns with gates and bars (verse 7) offered protection from raiders but became traps in a siege, which is why Saul thinks David has shut himself in.

Consulting God through the ephod usually took the form of yes-or-no questions, and the questions in verses 10 to 12 follow that pattern: one question at a time, each receiving a brief answer. The Ziphites were fellow members of the tribe of Judah, David's own tribe, and their willingness to hand him over shows that tribal loyalty was no guarantee of safety. Saul's warm blessing of the informers (verse 21) and his complaint that no one had shown him compassion reveal how isolated and self-pitying he has become.
literary: The chapter has three episodes: Keilah (verses 1 to 13), Jonathan's visit (verses 14 to 18), and the Ziphites' betrayal ending in the narrow escape at Maon (verses 19 to 29). Each episode turns on the question of whose hand David will fall into, and the word hand runs through the chapter: the LORD will deliver the Philistines into David's hand, Saul thinks God has delivered David into his hand, the people of Keilah would deliver him into Saul's hand, and the narrator states plainly that God would not deliver David into Saul's hand (verse 14). Jonathan's visit sits at the center, a moment of rest between two betrayals. The final scene is told with rising tension, Saul on one side of the mountain and David on the other, and the rescue comes suddenly and from an unexpected source.

outline.t: David inquires of the LORD and saves Keilah
The ephod warns David to leave Keilah
The Ziphites betray David to Saul
The chase around the mountain and the Philistine raid

doctrines.note: David inquires of the LORD before acting, asks again when his men are afraid, and asks specific questions when danger comes. The chapter presents prayerful dependence on God's guidance as a mark of the faithful king.
“Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand.” The Philistine raid at just the right moment shows God protecting David through events outside anyone's control.

Jonathan “strengthened his hand in God.” Encouragement here does not mean making David feel better but pointing him to God's promise, that he will be king. Faith is strengthened by being reminded of what God has said.

words.note: Sha'al, to ask or inquire. David asks the LORD repeatedly in this chapter. The same verb appears in Saul's name (Sha'ul, asked for), and in the people's asking for a king (8:10; 12:13). The king Israel asked for no longer asks God, while David does.

Chazaq, to be strong or to strengthen. Jonathan strengthened David's hand in God. The phrase echoes 30:6, where David, at his lowest point, strengthens himself in the LORD his God. The strength comes from God, not from the encourager.

Yasha, to save. The LORD tells David to go and save Keilah, and the narrator confirms that he did. The one anointed to be king acts as Israel's deliverer, a role Saul had been given and is no longer fulfilling.
Sela, rock or crag. David goes down to the rock in the Wilderness of Maon, and the place is later named the rock of escape. The Psalms often call God a rock, a place of refuge in danger.

christ: Jesus, like David, was rejected by many of the people he came to serve and was handed over by those who should have protected him. The Gospels describe him as one who prayed before every major decision and who depended on his Father's guidance (Luke 6:12-13; John 5:19). These are thematic connections rather than predictions, but they belong to the same story. Jonathan's words to David, pointing him to God's promise that he would be king, also show the shape of Christian encouragement in the New Testament, which strengthens believers by reminding them of what God has promised in Christ (Hebrews 10:23-25).

hard.q: God said Saul would come and that the people of Keilah would hand David over, but neither happened. How can God's answers be true if the events never took place?
hard.a: The LORD's answers describe what would have happened if David had stayed in Keilah. David left, so Saul did not come and the townspeople never had the chance to betray him. Theologians have discussed passages like this for centuries because they seem to show God knowing what free people would do under conditions that never arise. Some, often called Molinists after the sixteenth-century Jesuit Luis de Molina, see here evidence that God has knowledge of such conditional possibilities and uses it in guiding events. Others, including many Reformed and Thomist theologians, explain it differently, holding that God knows all things through his own decree and understanding rather than through a separate category of knowledge. Some open theists read the answers as God's accurate reading of present intentions and dispositions. These are second-order debates among Christians. The chapter's plain teaching is that God knew the danger David could not see and warned him in time.

questions: David asked God again when his men were afraid. What would it look like for you to seek God's direction a second time instead of giving in to fear?
Jonathan strengthened David's hand in God. Who in your life needs that kind of encouragement, and how could you give it?
The people David rescued would have betrayed him. How do you continue to serve people when you cannot count on their loyalty?
